dialogue.literal_gloss: Kana [if / when / or] • tapedza [finish] • izvi [this] • tichazorora [we will rest] • todya [let's eat] • zvakanaka [well / nicely] • tese. [all of us]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('tichazorora')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'tichazorora' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -cha- + Verb Stem = Future ('will') -> Ndichaenda (I will go), Vachadzoka (They will return)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

cultural_notes.title: Sharing a Meal Together ('Todya Zvakanaka Tese') After Collective Work
cultural_notes.content: In both family life and traditional communal work parties ('nhimbe' or 'humwe'), completing a shared task is always followed by resting in the shade and sharing a hearty meal together ('todya zvakanaka tese').

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Tiri kuronga rwendo rwemangwana rwekuenda Harare.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!

Rhino Conservation ('Zvipembere') in Zimbabwe's National Parks: Zimbabwe is one of Southern Africa's most important strongholds for both the black and white rhinoceros ('chipembere', plural 'zvipembere'), protected in sanctuaries such as Matobo National Park, Hwange, and the Lowveld conservancies..

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('masikati')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'masikati'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). grammar_notes.content: The verb 'ndinokumbira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Expressing 'Has/Have' and 'There Is/Are' ('-ne' & 'pane / kune')
grammar_notes.content: Shona does not use a separate verb like 'have'; instead, it combines a subject prefix with '-ne' ('with'). For people: 'ndine' (I have), 'une' (you have), 'ane' (he/she has), 'tine' (we have), 'vane' (they have). For things, the prefix matches the object: 'imba ine...' ('the house has...'), 'rori rine...' ('the truck has...'). When combined with the location prefixes 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-', it means 'there is / there are': 'pane' ('there is right here'), 'kune' ('there is in that area'), and 'mune' ('there is inside').
grammar_notes.rule: Person/Thing + -ne = has/have (tine = we have, ine = it has) | pane / kune / mune = there is / there are

If an elder's 'tsvimbo' drops to the ground, a younger person immediately picks it up ('kuinhonga') and hands it back with both hands.

grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakavhuvhuta' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nesimba'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nesimba'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'simba' forms 'nesimba'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Mhepo yakavhuvhuta nesimba, miti ikazununguka.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kuzorora')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kuzorora' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

cultural_notes.title: Clear Communication Across Open Spaces & Mobile Calls
cultural_notes.content: Whether speaking across a breezy homestead courtyard or over a mobile phone line with faint reception, checking 'Uri kunzwa zvakanaka here?' ('Can you hear clearly?') ensures nothing is lost in conversation.

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('ndinotanga')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'ndinotanga' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('kubasa')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kubasa'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'chirongwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'chirongwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Miombo Woodlands ('Masango eMusasa') & Botanical Observation in Zimbabwe: Central Zimbabwe lies within the southern African Miombo woodland belt, alongside homestead fruit trees such as avocado ('muti wemukotopeya'), mango, and banana ('mibhanana').

Sharing a Meal Together ('Todya Zvakanaka Tese') After Collective Work: In both family life and traditional communal work parties ('nhimbe' or 'humwe'), completing a shared task is always followed by resting in the shade and sharing a hearty meal together ('todya zvakanaka tese')..

Perseverance in Education ('Kupedza Chikoro') Against the Odds: Completing one's education ('kupedza chikoro') despite financial or practical hardships ('kunyangwe zvainetsa') is deeply admired across Zimbabwe, where families make immense sacrifices to see their children graduate..
Traditional Shona Ethnobotany & Leaf Observation: Shona elders possess an intimate knowledge of plant anatomy ('mashizha netsinga dzawo').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakadzima')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakadzima' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('yangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'yangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Linking Ideas Smoothly with 'saka'
grammar_notes.content: Longer Shona sentences flow naturally by linking two clauses with connectors like 'saka'. The four essential connectors to master are: 'uye' ('and / furthermore' between two clauses), 'asi' ('but / however'), 'saka' ('so / therefore'), and 'nokuti' / 'nekuti' ('because').
grammar_notes.rule: Clause 1 + [uye (and) | asi (but) | saka (so/therefore) | nokuti (because)] + Clause 2

cultural_notes.title: Mobile Phone Batteries ('Bhatiri reFoni') & Solar Charging
cultural_notes.content: When a mobile phone battery runs flat ('foni yakadzima bhatiri'), people politely explain why they missed messages ('mashoko'), and many households across urban and rural Zimbabwe use rooftop solar panels to keep phones and lights charged.

title: Chidzidzo 208: Ngatitangei zvino tisati tapedzerwa nguva nezvimwe...
shona_text: Ngatitangei zvino tisati tapedzerwa nguva nezvimwe zvinhu.

dialogue.speaker: Mutauri
dialogue.shona: Ngatitangei zvino tisati tapedzerwa nguva nezvimwe zvinhu.
dialogue.english: Let us start now before our time is taken up by other things.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ngatitangei [let's get started] • zvino [now] • tisati [before] • tapedzerwa [we are finished] • nguva [time / season] • nezvimwe [etc] • zvinhu. [things / items]

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nezvimwe'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nezvimwe'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'zvimwe' forms 'nezvimwe'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'tapedzerwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'tapedzerwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

cultural_notes.title: Valuing Time ('Nguva') & Collective Initiative ('Ngatitangei!')
cultural_notes.content: Using the inclusive exhortative prefix 'Nga-ti-...-i' ('Ngatitangei!'—'Let us begin right now!') rallies a group to make the most of the morning hours before other duties demand attention.

dialogue.english: I am very happy to see you again after so many days.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndafara [i'm happy] • zvikuru [very much / greatly] • kukuona [to see you] • zvakare [again] • mushure [after] • memazuva [of days] • akawanda. [many / numerous]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakare')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakare' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kukuona')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kukuona' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvikuru')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvikuru'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Warm Reunions ('Ndafara Zvikuru Kukuona') After Time Apart
cultural_notes.content: Reuniting with a relative or old friend after a long absence ('mushure memazuva akawanda') is celebrated with warm handshakes, smiles, and the heartfelt greeting 'Ndafara zvikuru kukuona zvakare!' ('I am overjoyed to see you again!').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akatonga')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akatonga' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Unogona')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Unogona' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('munyika')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'munyika'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').

grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'wangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

title: Chidzidzo 45: Rwizi rweZambezi rwuripamuganhu peZimbabwe neZambia

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'neZambia'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'neZambia'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'Zambia' forms 'neZambia'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Rwizi rweZambezi rwuripamuganhu peZimbabwe neZambia', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Describing Nouns: Word Order in Shona
grammar_notes.content: In English, descriptive words like adjectives, possessives ('my', 'our'), demonstratives ('this', 'that'), and numbers come BEFORE the noun ('this big house', 'my two books'). In Shona, the noun always comes FIRST, and all descriptive words follow right after it! For example: 'nyama iyi' ('this meat'), 'mwana uyu' ('this child'), 'goho guru' ('a big harvest'), and 'makomo marefu' ('tall mountains').
grammar_notes.rule: Noun FIRST + Descriptor SECOND -> mota iyi (this car), mabhuku edu (our books), makomo marefu (tall mountains)

cultural_notes.title: The Mighty Zambezi River ('Rwizi rweZambezi') & Victoria Falls ('Mosi-oa-Tunya')
cultural_notes.content: Forming the entire northern border between Zimbabwe and Zambia ('pamuganhu peZimbabwe neZambia'), the Zambezi River plunges over Victoria Falls ('Mosi-oa-Tunya' / 'Mapopoma eVictoria') and fills Lake Kariba, one of the world's largest man-made lakes.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakatanga')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakatanga' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'kudzvanyirirwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'kudzvanyirirwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('apo' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'apo') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: The Meaning of 'Chimurenga' & the Struggle Against Oppression
cultural_notes.content: The Shona word 'Chimurenga'—derived from the name of the legendary ancestor Murenga Sororenzou—signifies a collective struggle for justice, land, and freedom when people refuse to be oppressed ('vakaramba kudzvanyirirwa').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakatarwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakatarwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('mapako')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'mapako' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Expressing 'Has/Have' and 'There Is/Are' ('-ne' & 'pane / kune')
grammar_notes.content: Shona does not use a separate verb like 'have'; instead, it combines a subject prefix with '-ne' ('with'). For people: 'ndine' (I have), 'une' (you have), 'ane' (he/she has), 'tine' (we have), 'vane' (they have). For things, the prefix matches the object: 'imba ine...' ('the house has...'), 'rori rine...' ('the truck has...'). When combined with the location prefixes 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-', it means 'there is / there are': 'pane' ('there is right here'), 'kune' ('there is in that area'), and 'mune' ('there is inside').
grammar_notes.rule: Person/Thing + -ne = has/have (tine = we have, ine = it has) | pane / kune / mune = there is / there are

cultural_notes.title: Ancient San Rock Art in the Caves of the Matobo Hills ('Makomo eMatobo')
cultural_notes.content: A UNESCO World Heritage Site south of Bulawayo, the Matobo Hills ('Makomo eMatobo') feature dramatic balancing granite boulders and hundreds of rock shelters ('mapako') adorned with sacred paintings ('mifananidzo yakatarwa kare kare') created by San hunter-gatherers thousands of years ago.

grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kubasa'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('zvangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'zvangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

cultural_notes.content: Sitting quietly for a few minutes ('kugara pasi zvangu kwemaminitsi mashoma ndimbonyarara') is a valued way to unwind and gather one's thoughts after a lively day.

title: Chidzidzo 51: Kurova guva yaiva tsika yakakosha yekudzosa...
shona_text: Kurova guva yaiva tsika yakakosha yekudzosa mweya wemufi mumusha.
english_translation: The 'kurova guva' memorial ceremony was an important tradition for welcoming the spirit of the deceased back into the homestead.

dialogue.literal_gloss: Kurova [to beat] • guva [grave] • yaiva [it was] • tsika [culture] • yakakosha [it is important] • yekudzosa [of return] • mweya [spirit] • wemufi [of the deceased] • mumusha. [in the village]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakakosha')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakakosha' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mumusha')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mumusha'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('Kurova')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'Kurova' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: The Traditional Memorial Ceremony ('Kurova Guva' / 'Magadziko')
cultural_notes.content: In traditional Shona heritage, 'kurova guva' (also called 'magadziko' or 'chenura') was a solemn ceremony held about a year after an adult's passing to end the mourning period and symbolically welcome their protective ancestral spirit back to watch over the family homestead ('mumusha').

title: Chidzidzo 52: Unofunga kuti kurarama kwemazuva ekare kwaive...
shona_text: Unofunga kuti kurarama kwemazuva ekare kwaive nani pane kwanhasi here?

dialogue.literal_gloss: Unofunga [you/it thinking] • kuti [that / so that] • kurarama [to live] • kwemazuva [for days] • ekare [the old ones] • kwaive [it was] • nani [the better] • pane [there is / at] • kwanhasi [for today] • here? [(yes/no question marker)]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Unofunga')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Unofunga' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

cultural_notes.title: Intergenerational Conversations: Comparing Life Long Ago ('Mazuva Ekare') and Today
cultural_notes.content: Around the evening hearth or dinner table, elders and youth often debate how traditional life ('kurarama kwemazuva ekare')—with its organic foods, unhurried pace, and close-knit village solidarity—compares with modern technological life ('kwanhasi').

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nezviyo'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nezviyo'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'zviyo' forms 'nezviyo'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('vairima')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'vairima' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kurima')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kurima' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Indigenous Grains ('Mapfunde' & 'Zviyo') Before the Arrival of Maize ('Chibage')
cultural_notes.content: Long before maize ('chibage') was introduced from the Americas via Portuguese traders in the 16th and 17th centuries, the staple crops of Zimbabwe were indigenous drought-hardy sorghum ('mapfunde'), finger millet ('zviyo' / 'rukweza'), and pearl millet ('mhunga').

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('dzekukohwa')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'dzekukohwa' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Nziyo dzechinyakare dzayiimbwa panguva dzekukohwa kana parufu.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Traditional Shona Music ('Nziyo dzeChinyakare') from Harvest Joy to Mourning
cultural_notes.content: Traditional Shona songs ('nziyo dzechinyakare') accompanied every milestone of human life—from joyful communal work and harvest celebrations ('panguva dzekukohwa') to solemn songs of comfort and remembrance at funerals ('parufu').

cultural_notes.title: Fireside Folktales ('Ngano') of Tsuro Magen'a (the Clever Hare) & Gudo (the Baboon)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('aigara')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'aigara' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Lobengula aiva mambo wemaNdevere aigara muBulawayo panguva iyoyo.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Describing Nouns: Word Order in Shona
grammar_notes.content: In English, descriptive words like adjectives, possessives ('my', 'our'), demonstratives ('this', 'that'), and numbers come BEFORE the noun ('this big house', 'my two books'). In Shona, the noun always comes FIRST, and all descriptive words follow right after it! For example: 'nyama iyi' ('this meat'), 'mwana uyu' ('this child'), 'goho guru' ('a big harvest'), and 'makomo marefu' ('tall mountains').
grammar_notes.rule: Noun FIRST + Descriptor SECOND -> mota iyi (this car), mabhuku edu (our books), makomo marefu (tall mountains)

cultural_notes.title: King Lobengula & the Royal Capital of Bulawayo ('KoBulawayo')
cultural_notes.content: King Lobengula (son of King Mzilikazi, founder of the Ndebele Kingdom) ruled from his royal capital at Bulawayo in southwestern Zimbabwe during the late 19th century, a site preserved today at Old Bulawayo and the State House grounds.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('Vakadzi')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Vakadzi' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunotora')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunotora' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('dzavo')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'dzavo' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

cultural_notes.title: The Village Well ('Tsime') as a Space of Fellowship and Storytelling
cultural_notes.content: In rural communities, walking together to fetch cool water from the village spring or well ('kutsime') was a cherished daily social hour where women shared news, advice, and laughter along the footpath.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('vairemekedzwa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'vairemekedzwa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('rekupira')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'rekupira' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvikuru')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvikuru'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Ancestral Reverence ('Vadzimu') & Traditional Seven-Day Millet Brew
cultural_notes.content: In classical Shona cosmology, family ancestors ('vadzimu') were honoured as guardians who interceded with the Creator ('Musikavanhu' / 'Mwari'), and communities brewed seven-day finger-millet beer ('doro rezviyo') during thanksgiving ceremonies ('bira') for rain and family wellbeing.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akanyorwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akanyorwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('kuchikoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kuchikoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

cultural_notes.title: Studying the Mutapa Empire ('Umambo hweMutapa') in Zimbabwean Schools
cultural_notes.content: The Mutapa Empire ('Umambo hweMutapa'), founded in the 15th century in northern Zimbabwe and stretching toward the Zambezi Valley and Indian Ocean trade routes, is a centrepiece of history textbooks ('magwaro') in Zimbabwean schools.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('ndichaenda')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'ndichaenda' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)

Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.content:

• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('dzedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'dzedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

cultural_notes.title: Connecting Language, History ('Nhoroondo') & Cultural Identity ('Tsika')

In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'makwati' forms 'nemakwati'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('dzaishandisa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'dzaishandisa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('dzekurapa')

Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').

cultural_notes.title: Indigenous Herbal Medicine: Healing with Roots ('Midzi') & Bark ('Makwati')

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakabva')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakabva' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoziva')

For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('munyika')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'munyika'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvikuru')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvikuru'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: The Title 'Munhumutapa' & the Mutapa State
cultural_notes.content: Adopted by King Nyatsimba Mutota and his successors in the 1400s, the royal title 'Munhumutapa' (adapted by early Portuguese chroniclers as 'Monomotapa') became famous across the world as a symbol of sovereignty in Southern Africa.

grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Vhenekera')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Vhenekera' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('wako')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'wako' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvikuru')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvikuru'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

title: Chidzidzo 80: Kugadzira masimbi kwaida hunyanzvi hukuru, hwaishandiswa...
shona_text: Kugadzira masimbi kwaida hunyanzvi hukuru, hwaishandiswa kugadzira mapfumo.

dialogue.speaker: Mutauri
dialogue.shona: Kugadzira masimbi kwaida hunyanzvi hukuru, hwaishandiswa kugadzira mapfumo.
dialogue.english: Forging iron required great craftsmanship, which was used to make spears.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Kugadzira [to create] • masimbi [metals] • kwaida [it was needed] • hunyanzvi [skills] • hukuru, [greatness] • hwaishandiswa [was used] • kugadzira [to create] • mapfumo. [spears]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('hwaishandiswa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'hwaishandiswa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'hwaishandiswa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'hwaishandiswa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('Kugadzira')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'Kugadzira' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

title: Chidzidzo 66: Madzitateguru edu aishandisa uta nemiseve kana...

english_translation: Our ancestors used bows and arrows when they went hunting in the forest.

dialogue.speaker: Mutauri
dialogue.shona: Madzitateguru edu aishandisa uta nemiseve kana vachienda kunovhima musango.
dialogue.english: Our ancestors used bows and arrows when they went hunting in the forest.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Madzitateguru [ancestors] • edu [ours] • aishandisa [he used] • uta [a bow] • nemiseve [with arrows] • kana [if / when / or] • vachienda [leaving] • kunovhima [hunting] • musango. [in the forest]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunovhima')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunovhima' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemiseve'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemiseve'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'miseve' forms 'nemiseve'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('Waswera')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'Waswera'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('tinogona')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'tinogona' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

cultural_notes.title: Phone Etiquette in Shona: Always Starting with 'Waswera Sei?'
cultural_notes.content: Even when making a quick phone call to arrange a meeting ('kusangana nhasi'), a Shona speaker never jumps straight to the request—they always open warmly with 'Waswera sei?' ('How have you spent the day?').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakakomberedzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakakomberedzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

For example, 'ne-' + 'madziro' forms 'nemadziro'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

cultural_notes.title: Royal Capitals ('Mizinda yaMadzimambo') & Dry-Stone Architecture

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('munyika')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'munyika'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('raiporofita')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'raiporofita' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Chaminuka aive svikiro guru raiporofita zvaizoitika munyika mazuva aiz...', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

title: Chidzidzo 81: Ndinokumbira kuti utore magwaro ose ari...
