grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), grey ('gireyi'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('maviri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'maviri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('kumusoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kumusoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'pachigaro' = on the chair, 'patafura' = on the table, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'mundiro' = in the plate, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (pachigaro) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akasiyana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akasiyana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.content: In traditional and modern Shona homes alike, seating arrangements ('kugara pachigaro') reflect age, kinship, and hospitality ('hunhu'). grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akaunganidzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akaunganidzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('machena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'machena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), grey ('gireyi'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Modern Home Architecture & Brick Masonry in Zimbabwe
cultural_notes.content: Contemporary Zimbabwean home construction pairs fitted wardrobes and tiled interiors with durable face-brick masonry ('zvidhinha zvitsvuku'). Zimbabwean bricklayers ('vavaki') are celebrated across the region for their precise craftsmanship in residential and commercial architecture.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akakora')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akakora' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'pachigaro' = on the chair, 'patafura' = on the table, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'mundiro' = in the plate, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (pachigaro) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nedzimwe'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nedzimwe'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'dzimwe' forms 'nedzimwe'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

title: Chidzidzo 175: Mukati memusika, mune vanhu vanofamba. Vamwe... (Dzokororo 25)

shona_text: Vanhu vazhinji varikufamba mudhorobha. Parutivi pane motokari dzizhinji dzirikufamba mumugwagwa uye rimwe divi rine zvivakwa zvakawanda zvakakura. Shangu idzo dzine ruvara rutema. Dzakagadzirwa nomucheka uyo unotatamuka uye dzakanyorwa neruvara ruchena necheparutivi padzo. Mabhuku akarongererwa kubva pasi achikwira kudenga ari pamasherufu mukati mechitoro chinotengeserwa zvinhu zvinoshandiswa mumahofisi kana muzvikoro uye masherufu aya akagadzirwa nemuti. Pamusika panotaridza kuti panotengeswa mitsvairo. Mitsvairo inogadzirwa nehuswa hunosungwa huri pamwe chete. Hunoshandiswa kutsvaira mumba, Kubvisa tsvina kana kutsvaira paruvazhe. Pane madzimai arikuita basa iri.
english_translation: Many people are walking in town. On one side there are many cars on the road and on the other side there are many large buildings. Those shoes are black in color. They are made of stretchy fabric and are written in white on the side. Books are arranged from the ground up to the sky on the shelves inside a store that sells items used in offices or schools and these shelves are made of wood. In the market it appears that brooms are sold. Brooms are made of grass that is tied together. It is used to sweep the house, remove waste or sweep the yard. There are women doing this work.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakawanda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakawanda' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unotatamuka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unotatamuka' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Dignified Dress ('Kushambidzika') & Footwear in Zimbabwean Daily Life
cultural_notes.content: Across Zimbabwe, personal presentation ('kushambidzika') is treated as a visible expression of self-respect and respect for others. Whether wearing canvas sneakers ('shangu yetenisi'), flat walking shoes ('butsu'), or heeled dress shoes ('shangu dzine chitsiko chakakwirira'), Zimbabweans take pride in clean, well-kept footwear.
